claim: Dominant motor control theories propose that the brain predicts and attenuates the somatosensory consequences of actions, referred to as somatosensory attenuation.
source: Dominant motor control theories propose that the brain predicts and attenuates the somatosensory consequences of actions, referred to as somatosensory attenuation.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established motor control theories in the literature.

claim: Touch applied on a passive hand elicits attenuated perceptual and neural responses if it is actively generated by one's other hand, compared to an identical touch from an external origin.
source: Support comes from psychophysical and neuroimaging studies showing that touch applied on a passive hand elicits attenuated perceptual and neural responses if it is actively generated by one's other hand, compared to an identical touch from an external origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to psychophysical and neuroimaging studies.

claim: The perceived intensity of touch on the passive hand is enhanced if the active hand does not receive touch simultaneously with the passive hand (somatosensory enhancement).
source: However, recent experimental findings have challenged this view by providing psychophysical evidence that the perceived intensity of touch on the passive hand is enhanced if the active hand does not receive touch simultaneously with the passive hand (somatosensory enhancement)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent experimental findings.

claim: Attenuation has been attributed to the double tactile stimulation of the hands upon contact.
source: and by further attributing attenuation to the double tactile stimulation of the hands upon contact.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent experimental findings.

claim: Action does not enhance the predicted touch (Experiment 1).
source: In three pre-registered experiments, we demonstrate that action does not enhance the predicted touch (Experiment 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: The previously reported 'enhancement' effects are driven by the reference condition used (Experiment 2).
source: that the previously reported 'enhancement' effects are driven by the reference condition used (Experiment 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: Self-generated touch is robustly attenuated regardless of whether the two hands make contact (Experiment 3).
source: and that self-generated touch is robustly attenuated regardless of whether the two hands make contact (Experiment 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Action does not enhance but attenuates predicted touch.
source: Our results provide conclusive evidence that action does not enhance but attenuates predicted touch
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data from all three experiments.

claim: The brain uses an internal forward model in combination with a copy of the motor command (efference copy) to predict the sensory consequences of our movements.
source: Dominant motor control theories propose that the brain uses an internal forward model in combination with a copy of the motor command (efference copy) to predict the sensory consequences of our movements (McNamee and Wolpert, 2019; Shadmehr et al., 2008; Wolpert and Flanagan, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to motor control theories.

claim: The brain predicts the upcoming touch as one reaches toward an object.
source: For example, the brain predicts the upcoming touch as one reaches toward an object.
evidence: This claim is an example illustrating the application of forward models.

claim: Predictions allow for the correction of motor errors without relying on sensory feedback that suffers from intrinsic delays.
source: These predictions allow for the correction of motor errors without relying on sensory feedback that suffers from intrinsic delays (Shadmehr et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to motor control literature.

claim: Predictions improve the estimation of the current state of our body by combining the predicted touch with the actual sensory input.
source: thereby improving the estimation of the current state of our body by combining the predicted touch with the actual sensory input (Scott, 2004; Shadmehr et al., 2008; Todorov and Jordan, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to motor control literature.

claim: Predictions attenuate the perception of the self-generated input (sensory reafference) compared to that of externally generated input.
source: These predictions attenuate the perception of the self-generated input (sensory reafference) compared to that of externally generated input (Davidson and Wolpert, 2005; Franklin and Wolpert, 2011; Wolpert and Kawato, 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to motor control literature.

claim: Predictions allow to infer whether the cause of the sensory input is the self or the environment.
source: and allow to infer whether the cause of the sensory input is the self or the environment (Brown et al., 2013; Corlett, 2020; Idei et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: We are unable to tickle ourselves with our own touch, yet we are easily tickled by the touch of others.
source: A classic example of this attenuation is that we are unable to tickle ourselves with our own touch, yet we are easily tickled by the touch of others (Blakemore et al., 2000a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental evidence.

claim: The attenuation of sensory reafference is thought to be necessary to compensate for the limited capacity of the sensory systems by optimally prioritizing the perception of more informative externally generated stimuli.
source: The attenuation of sensory reafference – also referred to as sensory cancelation – is thought to be necessary to compensate for the limited capacity of the sensory systems by optimally prioritizing the perception of more informative externally generated stimuli (Bays and Wolpert, 2008; McNamee and Wolpert, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical literature.

claim: The attenuation model proposes that we dampen perceptual representations of expected self-generated stimuli to reduce redundancy and to highlight behaviorally relevant unexpected externally generated stimuli.
source: Thus, the attenuation model proposes that we dampen perceptual representations of expected self-generated stimuli to reduce redundancy and to highlight behaviorally relevant unexpected externally generated stimuli.
evidence: This claim summarizes the attenuation model based on cited literature.

claim: An alternative theoretical framework proposes that predictions, including those arising from our motor commands, should not attenuate but instead enhance sensory signals.
source: In contrast, an alternative theoretical framework proposes that predictions, including those arising from our motor commands, should not attenuate but instead enhance sensory signals, thereby allowing for sharper (i.e. more accurate) representations of predicted compared to unpredicted sensory events (Press et al., 2020; Press and Yon, 2019; Yon et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the enhancement model literature.

claim: The enhancement account posits that predictions based on our motor commands are equivalent to expectations formed by statistical regularities in sensory input or from prior knowledge.
source: This enhancement account – also referred to as the sharpening account – posits that predictions based on our motor commands are equivalent to expectations formed by statistical regularities in sensory input or from prior knowledge (e.g. at the North Pole, one expects to see a polar bear rather than an elephant)
evidence: This claim describes the enhancement account based on cited literature.

claim: Weak, noisy, or ambiguous sensory input that is in line with prior expectations should be enhanced to achieve, on average, more accurate representations.
source: and that these predictions should bias our perception towards our expectations. The proposal mainly stems from experimental research outside the domain of action and argues that weak, noisy, or ambiguous sensory input that is in line with prior expectations should be enhanced to achieve, on average, more accurate representations.
evidence: This claim is based on the enhancement model and cited research.

claim: We are more biased to report the presence of visual events that are statistically likely to occur rather than unlikely events.
source: For example, we are more biased to report the presence of visual events that are statistically likely to occur rather than unlikely events (Chalk et al., 2010; Wyart et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to visual perception studies.

claim: We are more sensitive to low-level visual features that are in line with prior expectations.
source: more sensitive to low-level visual features that are in line with prior expectations (Stein and Peelen, 2015; Teufel et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to visual perception studies.

claim: We show greater biases when perceiving visual events that are congruent with our expectations.
source: and show greater biases when perceiving visual events that are congruent with our expectations (Hudson et al., 2016a; Hudson et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to visual perception studies.

claim: Such effects are thought to result from mechanisms that increase the 'gain' of expected information by altering the weights of different sensory signals.
source: Such effects are thought to result from mechanisms that increase the 'gain' of expected information by altering the weights of different sensory signals (Summerfield and de Lange, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical literature.

claim: The enhancement model proposes that we amplify the perceptual representations of expected compared to unexpected sensory input.
source: Thus, the enhancement model proposes that we amplify the perceptual representations of expected compared to unexpected sensory input.
evidence: This claim summarizes the enhancement model based on cited literature.

claim: Touch delivered to one (passive) hand by the other (active) hand (i.e. self-generated touch) is perceived as weaker or less ticklish compared to a touch of identical intensity applied on the passive hand that is externally generated.
source: In the somatosensory domain, evidence supporting the attenuation model has repeatedly shown that touch delivered to one (passive) hand by the other (active) hand (i.e. self-generated touch) is perceived as weaker or less ticklish (Asimakidou et al., 2022; Bays et al., 2006; Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 1999; Kilteni et al., 2021; Kilteni et al., 2020; Kilteni et al., 2019; Kilteni et al., 2018; Kilteni and Ehrsson, 2022; Kilteni and Ehrsson, 2017a; Kilteni and Ehrsson, 2017b; Knoetsch and Zimmermann, 2021; McNaughton et al., 2023; Weiskrantz et al., 1971; Wolpe et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple psychophysical studies.

claim: Self-generated touch evokes attenuated somatosensory cortical activation compared to externally generated touch.
source: and evokes attenuated somatosensory cortical activation (Blakemore et al., 1998a; Hesse et al., 2010; Kilteni and Ehrsson, 2020; Shergill et al., 2014; Shergill et al., 2013) compared to a touch of identical intensity applied on the passive hand that is externally generated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: The action of the active hand results in an increase in the perceived intensity of touch on the passive hand, provided that the active hand never receives touch simultaneously with the passive hand.
source: In contrast, evidence supporting the enhancement model has shown that the action of the active hand results in an increase in the perceived intensity of touch on the passive hand, provided that the active hand never receives touch simultaneously with the passive hand (i.e. hands do not make contact) (Thomas et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study reporting enhancement effects.

claim: This enhancement finding has been recently used to support the sharpening model and to argue that attenuation effects are due to unspecific gating processes caused by the simultaneous double tactile stimulation of the two hands rather than action prediction.
source: This enhancement finding has been recently used to support the sharpening model and to argue that attenuation effects are due to unspecific gating processes caused by the simultaneous double tactile stimulation of the two hands rather than action prediction (Press et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a theoretical paper.

claim: Clarifying how predictions about the sensory consequences of our movements affect our perception is fundamental to understanding the interaction between perception and action.
source: Clarifying how predictions about the sensory consequences of our movements affect our perception is fundamental to understanding the interaction between perception and action (McNamee and Wolpert, 2019; Shadmehr et al., 2008; Wolpert and Flanagan, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to motor control theories.

claim: Clarifying how predictions affect perception is important for clinical and neurobiological theories of psychosis spectrum disorders, such as schizophrenia.
source: but also for clinical and neurobiological theories of psychosis spectrum disorders, such as schizophrenia (Blakemore et al., 2000b; Corlett et al., 2019; Frith, 2005a; Frith, 2005b; Frith, 2019; Frith et al., 2000; Shergill et al., 2014; Shergill et al., 2005) and schizotypy (Asimakidou et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Clarifying how predictions affect perception is important for understanding functional movement disorders.
source: as well as functional movement disorders (Pareés et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: Clarifying how predictions affect perception is important for understanding Parkinson's disease.
source: Parkinson's disease (Wolpe et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: Clarifying how predictions affect perception is important for understanding aging.
source: and aging (Wolpe et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: Thirty naïve participants participated in Experiment 1.
source: Thirty naïve participants moved their right index finger towards their left index finger to generate the touch on their left index finger with (contact condition) or without (no-contact condition) simultaneous stimulation on their active finger.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and sample size.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants moved their right index finger towards their left index finger to generate the touch on their left index finger with (contact condition) or without (no-contact condition) simultaneous stimulation on their active finger.
source: Thirty naïve participants moved their right index finger towards their left index finger to generate the touch on their left index finger with (contact condition) or without (no-contact condition) simultaneous stimulation on their active finger.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental conditions.

claim: A baseline condition in which the participants did not move their right index finger and received touch on the left index finger passively (externally generated touch) was included in Experiment 1.
source: A baseline condition in which the participants did not move their right index finger and received touch on the left index finger passively (externally generated touch) was included in order to distinguish between effects of attenuation or enhancement (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim describes the baseline condition and references Figure 1A.

claim: In Experiment 1, the PSEs were significantly lower in the contact condition than in the baseline condition (W = 422.00, p<0.001, rrb = 0.82, CI95 = [0.08, 0.25]).
source: The results showed a robust attenuation of the perceived touch when the two fingers made contact (contact condition) (Figure 1D, E and F): the PSEs were significantly lower in the contact condition than in the baseline condition (W = 422.00, p<0.001, rrb = 0.82, CI95 = [0.08, 0.25]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 1D, E, and F.

claim: In Experiment 1, the PSEs were significantly lower in the contact condition than in the no-contact condition (W = 441.00, p<0.001, rrb = 0.90, CI95 = [0.13, 0.26]).
source: Similarly, the PSEs were significantly lower in the contact condition than in the no-contact condition (W = 441.00, p<0.001, rrb = 0.90, CI95 = [0.13, 0.26]) (Figure 1D, E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 1D, E, and G.

claim: In Experiment 1, the no-contact condition did not produce any significant change in the perceived magnitude of the touch compared to the baseline condition (W = 187.00, p=0.360, rrb = –0.20, CI95 = [–0.08, 0.030]).
source: Critically, however, in the comparison that contrasts the hypotheses of the two models, the no-contact condition did not produce any significant change in the perceived magnitude of the touch compared to the baseline condition (W = 187.00, p=0.360, rrb = –0.20, CI95 = [–0.08, 0.030]) (Figure 1D, E and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 1D, E, and H.

claim: A Bayesian factor analysis provided moderate support for the absence of any difference between no-contact and baseline conditions in Experiment 1 (BF01 = 3.58).
source: A Bayesian factor analysis provided moderate support for the absence of any difference (BF01 = 3.58).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1, the JNDs did not significantly differ between any of the conditions (all p>0.05).
source: In Experiment 1, the JNDs did not significantly differ between any of the conditions (all p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Experiment 1 does not support the hypothesis of the enhancement model that action enhances predicted touch but supports the hypothesis of the attenuation model.
source: In summary, we used both frequentist and Bayesian statistics and found no evidence that the action of the right index finger produces an enhancement of the touch received on the left index finger when the fingers did not make contact, relative to the baseline. Thus, Experiment 1 does not support the hypothesis of the enhancement model that action enhances predicted touch but supports the hypothesis of the attenuation model.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: Thirty new naïve participants participated in Experiment 2.
source: Thirty new naïve participants participated in Experiment 2, which included a block of contact trials and a block of no-contact trials in which participants moved their right index finger, but each block also contained randomly intermixed NOGO trials where participants were cued to withhold their movement, identical to the design of Thomas et al., 2022 (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and sample size, and references Figure 2A.

claim: In Experiment 2, each block contained randomly intermixed NOGO trials where participants were cued to withhold their movement, identical to the design of Thomas et al., 2022.
source: Thirty new naïve participants participated in Experiment 2, which included a block of contact trials and a block of no-contact trials in which participants moved their right index finger, but each block also contained randomly intermixed NOGO trials where participants were cued to withhold their movement, identical to the design of Thomas et al., 2022 (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and references a previous study and Figure 2A.

claim: If the previously reported enhancement effects are due to the baseline used, attenuated perception of touch during the motor inhibition condition (i.e. NOGO trials) should be found compared to the baseline.
source: If the previously reported enhancement effects are due to the baseline used, attenuated perception of touch during the motor inhibition condition (i.e. NOGO trials) should be found compared to the baseline, which would then lead to apparent enhancement effects upon comparison with the no-contact trials (Figure 2B and C) (Methods).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis tested in Experiment 2 and references Figure 2B and C.

claim: In Experiment 2, all the effects of Experiment 1 were replicated in the new sample.
source: This hypothesis (Figure 2B) was confirmed. First, all the effects of Experiment 1 were replicated in the new sample (Figure 2D, E and F & H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 and references Figure 2D, E, F, and H.

claim: In Experiment 2, the contact trials yielded significant attenuation (i.e. lower PSEs) compared to the baseline condition (t(29) = 6.79, p<0.001, d = 1.24, CI95 = [0.18, 0.33]).
source: The contact trials yielded significant attenuation (i.e. lower PSEs) compared to the baseline condition (t(29) = 6.79, p<0.001, d = 1.24, CI95 = [0.18, 0.33]) (Figure 2E & H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2E and H.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was no enhancement in the no-contact trials compared to the baseline condition (t(29) = 0.45, p=0.658, d = 0.08, CI95 = [–0.05, 0.07]).
source: Once again, there was no enhancement in the no-contact trials compared to the baseline condition (t(29) = 0.45, p=0.658, d = 0.08, CI95 = [–0.05, 0.07]) (Figure 2D & F)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2D and F.

claim: In Experiment 2, the Bayesian analysis yielded moderate evidence for the absence of any effects between no-contact and baseline (BF01 = 4.69).
source: and the Bayesian analysis again yielded moderate evidence for the absence of any effects (BF01 = 4.69).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 2, the PSEs in the NOGO (motor inhibition) trials were significantly lower than the baseline condition both for the contact NOGO (t(29) = 2.99, p=0.006, d = 0.55, CI95 = [0.02, 0.09]) and the no-contact NOGO trials (t(29) = 4.44, p<0.001, d = 0.81, CI95 = [0.05, 0.13]).
source: Importantly, the PSEs in the NOGO (motor inhibition) trials were significantly lower than the baseline condition both for the contact NOGO (t(29) = 2.99, p=0.006, d = 0.55, CI95 = [0.02, 0.09]) and the no-contact NOGO trials (t(29) = 4.44, p<0.001, d = 0.81, CI95 = [0.05, 0.13]) (Figure 2D and E & G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2D, E, and G.

claim: In Experiment 2, NOGO trials resulted in a suppression of perceived touch on the left hand.
source: This demonstrates that NOGO trials resulted in a suppression of perceived touch on the left hand.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the suppression in NOGO trials led to an apparent increase in the PSE of the no-contact trials compared to the NOGO trials in the no-contact block (t(29) = –2.98, p=0.006, d = –0.54, CI95 = [–0.12,–0.02]), mimicking an 'enhancement' effect.
source: Critically, this led to an apparent increase in the PSE of the no-contact trials compared to the NOGO trials in the no-contact block (t(29) = –2.98, p=0.006, d = –0.54, CI95 = [–0.12,–0.02]), mimicking an 'enhancement' effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, PSEs were significantly lower in the contact trials than in the NOGO trials (t(29) = 5.91, p<0.001, d = 1.08, CI95 = [0.13, 0.27]).
source: Finally, PSEs were significantly lower in the contact trials than in the NOGO trials (t(29) = 5.91, p<0.001, d = 1.08, CI95 = [0.13, 0.27])
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, the NOGO trials in the contact and no-contact blocks did not significantly differ (t(29) = 1.58, p=0.126, d = 0.29, CI95 = [–0.01, 0.08], BF01 = 1.697).
source: while the NOGO trials in the contact and no-contact blocks did not significantly differ (t(29) = 1.58, p=0.126, d = 0.29, CI95 = [–0.01, 0.08], BF01 = 1.697).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, the JNDs were not significantly different between conditions (p>0.05), except in the contact condition, where the JNDs were significantly higher than in the baseline condition (t(29) = –2.52, p=0.017, d = –0.46, CI95 = [–0.06,–0.01]).
source: In Experiment 2, the JNDs were not significantly different between conditions (p>0.05), except in the contact condition, where the JNDs were significantly higher than in the baseline condition (t(29) = –2.52, p=0.017, d = –0.46, CI95 = [–0.06,–0.01]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Experiment 2 does not support the hypothesis that action enhances predicted touch.
source: In summary, identical to Experiment 1, we used both frequentist and Bayesian statistics and did not find any evidence that the action of the right index finger produces an enhancement of the touch received on the left index finger when the fingers do not make contact, relative to the baseline. Moreover, we showed that the purported 'enhancement' effect (Thomas et al., 2022) is driven by a suppression of the perceived intensity of touch following a cue to inhibit the planned movement, both relative to the baseline and to the condition where the fingers do not make contact (no-contact). Thus, Experiment 2 does not support the hypothesis that action enhances predicted touch.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The purported 'enhancement' effect is driven by a suppression of the perceived intensity of touch following a cue to inhibit the planned movement.
source: Moreover, we showed that the purported 'enhancement' effect (Thomas et al., 2022) is driven by a suppression of the perceived intensity of touch following a cue to inhibit the planned movement, both relative to the baseline and to the condition where the fingers do not make contact (no-contact).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: Thirty new naïve participants participated in Experiment 3.
source: In Experiment 3, this hypothesis was explicitly tested with thirty new naïve participants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and sample size.

claim: In Experiment 3, the same contact and no-contact conditions were included as in Experiment 1, but their relative frequency was manipulated within the same block (contact trials: 80%, no-contact trials: 20%).
source: The same contact and no-contact conditions were included as in Experiment 1, but their relative frequency was manipulated within the same block (contact trials: 80%, no-contact trials: 20%) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and references Figure 3A.

claim: In Experiment 3, in the no-contact trials, the platform automatically retracted before trial onset, unbeknownst to the participants, leading them to unexpectedly miss the contact with the sensor but still trigger the test force only by the position of their right index finger.
source: In the contact trials, participants tapped the force sensor to trigger the test force identically to Experiments 1 and 2, but in the no-contact trials, the platform automatically retracted before trial onset, unbeknownst to the participants, leading them to unexpectedly miss the contact with the sensor but still trigger the test force only by the position of their right index finger.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental manipulation in Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, participants' vision was occluded so that they could not know whether the next trial would be a contact or a no-contact trial.
source: Participants' vision was occluded so that they could not know whether the next trial would be a contact or a no-contact trial.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental procedure.

claim: In Experiment 3, the results showed a robust attenuation in both contact and no-contact trials with respect to the baseline condition, regardless of whether contact was made.
source: The results showed a robust attenuation in both contact and no-contact trials with respect to the baseline condition, regardless of whether contact was made (Figure 3D, E and F & H)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 and references Figure 3D, E, F, and H.

claim: In Experiment 3, the PSEs were significantly lower in the contact condition than in the baseline condition (t(29) = 8.06, p<0.001, d = 1.47, CI95 = [0.16, 0.27]).
source: the PSEs were significantly lower in the contact condition than in the baseline condition (t(29) = 8.06, p<0.001, d = 1.47, CI95 = [0.16, 0.27])
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 3, the PSEs were lower in the no-contact condition than in the baseline condition (t(29) = 4.45, p<0.001, d = 0.81, CI95 = [0.07, 0.20]).
source: and lower in the no-contact condition than in the baseline condition (t(29) = 4.45, p<0.001, d = 0.81, CI95 = [0.07, 0.20]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 3, the magnitude of attenuation was larger in the contact condition than in the no-contact condition, with significantly lower PSEs in the contact condition than in the no-contact condition (t(29) = 3.94, p<0.001, d = 0.72, CI95 = [0.04, 0.12]).
source: The magnitude of attenuation was larger in the contact condition than in the no-contact condition, with significantly lower PSEs in the contact condition than in the no-contact condition (t(29) = 3.94, p<0.001, d = 0.72, CI95 = [0.04, 0.12]) (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 3G.

claim: In Experiment 3, the difference in the magnitude of attenuation between contact and no-contact conditions was modest (≅ 35%).
source: The difference in the magnitude of attenuation was modest (≅ 35%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: The findings of Experiment 3 indicate that the perceived intensity of touch on the passive left hand was significantly attenuated both when the active hand received touch or not, thereby ruling out the possibility that attenuation is merely due to simultaneous tactile stimulation.
source: These findings indicate that the perceived intensity of touch on the passive left hand was significantly attenuated both when the active hand received touch or not, thereby ruling out the possibility that attenuation is merely due to simultaneous tactile stimulation (Press et al., 2023; Thomas et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: The results of Experiment 3 emphasize the predictive nature of somatosensory attenuation, which is observed only when the sensorimotor context allows the formation of such predictions.
source: The results of Experiment 3 emphasize the predictive nature of somatosensory attenuation, which is observed only when the sensorimotor context allows the formation of such predictions.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiments 1 and 2 attenuation was only observed in the contact conditions, whereas attenuation was also observed in the no-contact condition of Experiment 3, where participants expected that they would make contact.
source: In Experiments 1 and 2 attenuation was only observed in the contact conditions, whereas attenuation was also observed in the no-contact condition of Experiment 3, where participants expected that they would make contact (i.e. the sensorimotor context was conducive to predicting self-touch).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from all three experiments.

claim: Larger differences between the PSEs in the contact and no-contact conditions were observed for Experiments 1 and 2 compared to Experiment 3.
source: Thus, larger differences between the PSEs in the contact and no-contact conditions were observed for Experiments 1 and 2 compared to Experiment 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data across experiments.

claim: Bonferroni corrected post hoc comparisons indicated significant differences between Experiments 1 and 3 (t(58) = 3.10, p=0.008, d = 0.80, CI95 = [0.03, 0.23]) as well as Experiments 2 and 3 (t(58) = 3.76, p<0.001, d = 0.97, CI95 = [0.06, 0.26]), but no significant differences between Experiments 1 and 2 (t(58) = –0.66, p=1.000, d = –0.17, CI95 = [–0.13, 0.07], BF01 = 3.308).
source: with Bonferroni corrected post hoc comparisons indicating significant differences between Experiments 1 and 3 (t(58) = 3.10, p=0.008, d = 0.80, CI95 = [0.03, 0.23]) as well as Experiments 2 and 3 (t(58) = 3.76, p<0.001, d = 0.97, CI95 = [0.06, 0.26]), but no significant differences between Experiments 1 and 2 (t(58) = –0.66, p=1.000, d = –0.17, CI95 = [–0.13, 0.07], BF01 = 3.308).
